preamble: A tribute to an old friend

clue.text: Driven thing, tough — and the best!

parts.note: hard means tough, as in a hard nut
the top is the best of anything, as in top of the class

explanation.surface: Someone praises a thing that is driven as tough and first-rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driven thing' sounds like a determined person; it is a car, something you drive.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardtop is a motor car with a rigid roof, a vehicle that gets driven.

clue.text: Holy man, nothing less, composed for service book

indicators.note: put together in a new arrangement
without, so the zero is taken out

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A holy man composes something for a church service book.
explanation.walkthrough: HOLYMAN less O gives HLYMAN, which 'composed' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A hymnal is a book of hymns used during church worship.

clue.text: Our final wish is a pretence, it turns out

indicators.note: the letters are turned out in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a final wish was just pretence.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is the traditional farewell to the dead, here offered to the setter.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the customary wish for someone who has died, the last thing said over them.

clue.text: In match, start to play with clubs in a calculated way

indicators.note: placed inside, so the following pieces go within the match

parts.note: to tally is to match or agree
Act I is the start of a play
C is clubs in card notation

explanation.surface: In a sports match, starting the game with clubs is a strategic move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start to play' is not a first letter: it is ACT I, the opening act.
explanation.definitionFit: Tactically means done with careful planning, as a calculated move would be.

clue.text: Uncomplicated man of the cloth spilling his tea

indicators.note: he loses his own drink, so it comes out of his title

parts.note: a chaplain is a clergyman
cha is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A plain-spoken clergyman knocks over his cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA, British slang for tea, comes out of CHAPLAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain means simple and straightforward, without fuss.

clue.text: This unusually fruitful giant outstanding at finding inspiration for starters

indicators.note: standing outside, so the giant's letters go round the others

parts.note: Gog is a legendary giant, of Gog and Magog
taken as written

indicators.note: the opening letters of the two words before it are taken

explanation.surface: A tribute to a giant setter whose inspiration was unusually fruitful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' reads as praise but means standing out, around AT and FI.
explanation.definitionFit: The goat fig, or caprifig, is the wild fig whose wasps pollinate cultivated figs, making it unusually useful for fruiting.

clue.text: Reverend's ultimate parting gift, setters' youthful education of old

indicators.note: splitting apart the gift so the letter goes inside

parts.note: a grant is a gift of money

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the setters speaking of themselves say our

explanation.surface: The Reverend leaves a final gift to the setters who learnt from him in youth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parting gift' reads as a farewell present; 'parting' splits GRANT round D, the last of Reverend's.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grand Tour was the long European trip that rounded off a young gentleman's education in earlier centuries.

clue.text: A vicar finally getting his place above all others

indicators.note: the last letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the vicar's place is the church, CH

explanation.surface: A vicar at last gets his place of supreme honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Arch as an adjective means chief or principal, ranking first.

clue.text: Drop round — we're sorry to say goodbye …

indicators.note: going around, so the drop encloses the rest

parts.note: to fall is to drop

indicators.note: in a sorry state, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: Someone drops in and says how sad it is to part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sorry' looks like regret but jumbles WERE to AREWE inside FALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell is a parting word, said on leaving.

clue.text: … but we fitted much of 10 in, Dei gratia

indicators.note: put together in a new arrangement
a good part of the name, its opening letters, with the rest cut

parts.note: the setter's name at 10 across
taken as written
Latin for by the grace of God, abbreviated DG on British coins

explanation.surface: The newspaper says it fitted the setter in by the grace of God.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we' is the newspaper speaking of itself, following on from 7 down. ARAU, IN and DG are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guardian is the newspaper that printed this puzzle, referring to itself.

clue.text: Such a noted art I'm not sure returns thus

indicators.note: comes back, so the hesitation noise is read backwards

parts.note: um is the noise of hesitation, saying I'm not sure
sic is Latin for thus, used to mark a quotation as printed

explanation.surface: A hesitant speaker doubts a celebrated art form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'noted' looks like 'famous' but means written in musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: This art is literally written down in notes on a stave, hence a noted one.

clue.text: Gilt-edged artist, foremost of compilers on song, our beloved hero

indicators.note: gold edges the artist, so the artist goes inside the gold

parts.note: gilt is gold, chemical symbol Au
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

indicators.note: the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: an aria is a song in opera

explanation.surface: A tribute to a golden artist, first among setters, the solvers' beloved hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gilt-edged' looks like a compliment; read as two parts it puts RA inside AU to make ARAU. 'on' simply sets the C beside ARIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Araucaria was the pseudonym of John Graham, the much-loved Guardian setter this puzzle honours.

clue.text: 10 across's ultimate invention that's timeless, followed by a complete devotee

indicators.note: the remaining pieces come after the first ones
the final letter of that pen-name is taken

parts.note: refers to the setter's pen-name at 10 across

indicators.note: without time, so the letter T for time is dropped

parts.note: fiction is invention, something made up
to do a job is to complete it

explanation.surface: The setter's final invention is timeless, and a complete devotee follows it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'timeless' sounds like praise but tells you to drop T from FICTION, leaving FICION. 'complete' is a verb here, giving DO.
explanation.definitionFit: An aficionado is a keen enthusiast or fan, someone devoted to a pursuit.

clue.text: Entertained by endless poetry, us solvers were indebted

indicators.note: held as a guest within, so the solvers' word sits inside the poetry
the last letter of the poem is cut off

parts.note: an ode is a poem, a piece of poetry
we, the solvers, speaking of ourselves

explanation.surface: Solvers, delighted by the setter's poetic touch, owed him a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' trims ODE to OD, and WE goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Owed is the past tense of owe, so were indebted means the same thing.

clue.text: Innovator holding up letter to show worthy opponent

indicators.note: the innovator's word holds the other inside it

parts.note: a changer is one who changes things, an innovator

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read upwards, backwards

parts.note: ell is the name of the letter L

explanation.surface: An innovator raises a letter to prove himself a rival worth facing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding up' looks like one phrase; 'holding' contains and 'up' reverses ELL to LLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A challenger is a contender who takes on a champion, a rival of note.

clue.text: Sort of nag, Shetland pony might you say, with a love of the country

indicators.note: a sort of nag means its letters are sorted into a new order
signals that the words are spoken, giving a sound-alike spelling

parts.note: a Shetland pony is a short horse, a low filly

explanation.surface: A horse-lover compares an old nag to a Shetland pony, a small breed from the Scottish isles.
explanation.walkthrough: The Shetland pony becomes 'low filly', spoken to give LOPHILI. 'with' joins the A on; 'the country' is England.
explanation.definitionFit: Anglophilia is admiration for England and its ways, a fondness for that country.

clue.text: Understanding devious hinter's in-joke?

indicators.note: placed inside, so the hinter goes inside the joke

parts.note: a gag is a joke

indicators.note: winding, so the letters take a crooked route

parts.note: a hinter is one who drops hints; the 's is read as is, linking to the containment

explanation.surface: Getting the private joke of someone who drops sly hints.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in-joke' looks like one word; HINTER is rearranged to THERIN and is placed in GAG.
explanation.definitionFit: Gathering can mean an inference, as when one says I gather, a form of understanding.

clue.text: Behave shiftily and selfishly? Not this self-effacing character!

parts.note: to hedge is to avoid committing, to be evasive
to behave selfishly is to hog things

explanation.surface: Someone acting evasively and greedily is the opposite of a modest character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behave' serves both pieces. 'Not this' points out the irony: the name sounds selfish but the creature is shy.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedgehog curls into a ball to hide, as a shy, retiring creature might.

clue.text: Rehearsal for card game finished by Spoonerist?

indicators.note: a speaker who swaps the opening sounds of two words, like Rev Spooner

parts.note: rummy is a card game
done means finished

explanation.surface: Someone practises a card game until a word-swapping speaker finishes it.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the opening sounds of 'rummy done' gives 'dummy run'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dummy run is a practice attempt, a trial before the real thing.

clue.text: Other characters are all quite square, possibly?

indicators.note: the same letters put in a different order become other characters

explanation.surface: Someone says the rest of the people are rather conventional, or square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'square' looks like slang for dull, but it is the shape with four equal sides.
explanation.definitionFit: A square is one example of a figure whose sides are all of equal length.

clue.text: Close of day for close companion

parts.note: Fri is the abbreviation for Friday
the close is the end

explanation.surface: The end of the day is a time for a close companion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close of day' is read as the end of a day, that is FRI followed by END.
explanation.definitionFit: A friend is someone you are close to and keep company with.

clue.text: Master standing to admit dereliction of duty in sanctum sanctorum

indicators.note: let in, so the master's letters go round the others
in a down clue, standing up means reading the letters upwards

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts

indicators.note: neglect of, so the letters fall out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A master stands accused of neglecting his duty in a holy place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standing' turns MA to AM, which admits DYTU, the jumbled 'duty'.
explanation.definitionFit: An adytum was the innermost shrine of an ancient temple, its holiest place.

clue.text: Spirited crossword, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: ... in the sense of plucky and willing, ready to have a go
a crossword is one example of a pastime played for fun

explanation.surface: A lively crossword puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: A plucky person is game, and a crossword is a kind of puzzle played as a pastime.

clue.text: Getting on, a parish priest with RAF ultimately feared lost was seen again

parts.note: re means on or about, as in a letter's subject line

indicators.note: the picked letter goes missing from the word before

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the final letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: An ageing parish priest, once feared lost with the air force, turned up again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' looks like ageing; 'on' gives RE. The last letter of RAF, F, is lost from FEARED, leaving EARED.
explanation.definitionFit: To reappear is to be seen once more after going missing.

clue.text: See 2
Nothing's better than faith and hope, according to Paul (and Enigmatist and Shed)

definitions.text: Nothing's better than faith and hope, according to Paul (and Enigmatist and Shed)

parts.words: Nothing's better than faith and hope, according to Paul (and Enigmatist and Shed)
parts.note: St Paul in Corinthians ranks charity above faith and hope; nothing is a zero score in tennis; Paul, Enigmatist and Shed are setters

explanation.surface: A biblical saying claimed by the apostle and also by three crossword setters.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul is both the apostle and a fellow Guardian setter, and the three named setters wrote this tribute together.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a zero score is called this, and St Paul says it outranks faith and hope.

clue.text: One decorated by monarch, perhaps, 8's responsibility to drop off award — I'll be blowed!

indicators.note: signals the letters may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral

indicators.note: the ward's letters fall away from the next word

parts.note: the answer to 8 down is a guardian, whose responsibility is a ward

explanation.surface: Someone honoured by the king is surprised to lose an award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I'll be blowed!' sounds like an exclamation of surprise; it is what a mouth organ might say. Taking WARD off AWARD leaves A, after HARMONIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A harmonica is played by blowing into it, so it could say this of itself.

clue.text: Much-respected rector tucking into good feed

indicators.note: going inside, so the rector's letter is put within the others

parts.note: to feed is to eat

explanation.surface: A respected clergyman enjoys a hearty meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' looks like eating, but it puts R inside G and EAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone great is eminent and widely admired.

clue.text: What may restore fount of knowledge from King's, after playing with some appropriate language

indicators.note: once played around with, the remaining letters are rearranged
taken away from, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: the word King's, with its S kept

indicators.note: the source, that is the first letter, of the next word

parts.note: English, the apt language here, abbreviated Eng

explanation.surface: A scholar from King's College finds a restorative remedy in fitting words.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove K, the start of 'knowledge', from KINGS; rearranging INGS gives GINS, then ENG follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginseng is a root taken as a tonic, believed to restore vitality.

clue.text: Attention given to fantastic old master's noble rank

parts.note: to give an ear is to pay attention

indicators.note: wild and fanciful, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for master, as in MA

explanation.surface: Someone gives ear to a wonderful old painter's title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old master' looks like a painter, but 'old' is anagrammed to LDO and 'master' gives M.
explanation.definitionFit: An earldom is the title and rank of an earl, a peer of the realm.
